description: Two examples of citizens working through groups to change public policy or challenge injustice.
content_html:
Why Case Studies Matter

The specification asks you to know two contrasting examples of how citizens working together have attempted to change or improve their communities. These examples should demonstrate different methods and different contexts, so that you can compare and evaluate how citizens use collective action to address public policy, challenge injustice or resolve a community issue. Citizenship action can be local, national or international, and can focus on issues from across the political spectrum.

This lesson examines two case studies: first, the Hillsborough families’ campaign for justice; second, the campaign by disability rights organisations that contributed to the Equality Act 2010. Both are factual accounts of civic action and its outcomes, presented as models of how citizens can make a difference through sustained, organised effort.

Case Study 1: The Hillsborough Families’ Campaign

On 15 April 1989, ninety-seven people died in a crush at Hillsborough football stadium in Sheffield during an FA Cup semi-final. (A ninety-eighth victim died in 2021.) The initial official narrative wrongly blamed supporters for the disaster. Families of those who died refused to accept this account and began a campaign for the truth and legal accountability.

The Hillsborough Family Support Group used a wide range of methods over more than three decades. They petitioned Parliament, gathered and preserved evidence, engaged solicitors and barristers, lobbied MPs and successive governments, and worked with journalists to keep the issue in the public eye. In 2012, the Hillsborough Independent Panel published a report showing that 96 victims were unlawfully killed and that there had been a cover-up by South Yorkshire Police and others.

Key Fact

The Hillsborough families used petitions, legal action, lobbying, media engagement and sustained public campaigning over more than 30 years. Key outcomes: the 2012 Independent Panel report confirmed unlawful killing; in 2016 the original inquest verdicts were quashed and a new inquest jury returned unlawful killing verdicts for 96 of the 97 victims.

The Hillsborough case illustrates several important citizenship principles. First, that ordinary citizens without formal political power can challenge state institutions and achieve justice through sustained, evidence-based campaigning. Second, that legal processes (inquests, judicial review, criminal investigation) are an important route alongside political pressure. Third, that the campaign required decades of perseverance and that meaningful change in complex cases takes time.

Case Study 2: Disability Rights and the Equality Act 2010

The Equality Act 2010 is a landmark piece of legislation that consolidated and strengthened protections against discrimination in the UK. It brought together previous laws on sex, race and disability discrimination and extended protection to nine protected characteristics. Its passage was shaped by decades of campaigning by disability rights organisations, women’s groups and equality bodies.

Disability rights organisations such as Scope and the Disability Rights Commission campaigned throughout the 1990s and 2000s for stronger legal protections. Their methods included direct advocacy to MPs and ministers, evidence submissions to parliamentary committees, public awareness campaigns, and legal challenges under existing equality legislation to test and extend its boundaries. The Disability Discrimination Act 1995 was an early result; the Equality Act 2010 consolidated and strengthened those rights further.

Key Fact

The Equality Act 2010 covers nine protected characteristics: age, disability, gender reassignment, marriage and civil partnership, pregnancy and maternity, race, religion or belief, sex, and sexual orientation. It applies to employment, education, housing and the provision of services.

This case study illustrates a different model of citizenship action. Rather than responding to a single injustice (as the Hillsborough families did), disability rights organisations pursued a long-term legislative strategy across multiple parliaments and governments. They combined insider tactics (formal consultations, committee evidence, working with sympathetic MPs) with outsider tactics (public campaigns and demonstrations), demonstrating that the two approaches are not mutually exclusive.

The Hillsborough and disability rights campaigns differ in several important ways. The Hillsborough campaign focused on a single specific injustice and pursued legal justice through the courts and inquests alongside political lobbying. The disability rights campaign pursued systemic legislative change across a wider range of issues and over a longer strategic timeline.

Both campaigns, however, share important features: they involved citizens working collectively rather than individually; they combined multiple methods (legal, political, media, public); they required persistence over years or decades; and they achieved tangible, lasting changes (the 2016 inquest verdicts; the Equality Act 2010). Both demonstrate that citizens can achieve meaningful outcomes even against powerful institutions, provided they are organised, evidence-based and persistent.

Evaluating Citizenship Actions

When you are asked to evaluate a citizenship action in the exam, you need to assess both process and outcome. Did the action achieve its stated aim? If not fully, did it make progress? Were the methods used appropriate and effective? What were the limitations or unintended consequences? A strong evaluation will consider impact from multiple perspectives — the citizens who took action, those the action was meant to help, and the wider democratic system.

Students often evaluate citizenship actions in binary terms — either “it worked” or “it failed”. Exam mark schemes reward more nuanced thinking. A campaign can partially succeed: it may change public awareness without changing law; it may change law without changing behaviour; it may achieve its immediate aim but reveal deeper structural problems. Strong evaluative answers assess what was achieved, what was not, and why — considering factors such as the resources available to the campaign, the political climate at the time, and whether the methods chosen matched the aims.
exam_tip_html: When you are asked to “describe” a citizenship action case study, give two clearly developed features — what the group did and what they achieved — with specific named details. When you “discuss” the effectiveness of citizens working through groups, use connectives (“however”, “on the other hand”) and name the specific case studies you have studied. For the 12-mark “evaluate”, a strong answer will weigh the methods against the outcomes for both case studies and reach a substantiated judgement about what makes collective citizenship action effective — not simply a list of what happened in each case.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Hillsborough families’ campaign shows how citizens can challenge institutions through sustained legal, political and media pressure, achieving unlawful killing verdicts for 96 victims after more than 30 years.
  • Disability rights campaigns demonstrate a long-term legislative strategy, contributing to the Equality Act 2010, which protects nine characteristics including disability, race, sex and religion.
  • Effective citizenship actions tend to combine multiple methods, involve collective rather than individual effort, and require persistence — meaningful change rarely happens quickly.

practice_questions.text:
The Equality Act 2010 protects citizens from discrimination on the basis of a number of 'protected characteristics'. Which of the following is NOT a protected characteristic under the Act?
A) Disability
B) Nationality of birth country
C) Religion or belief
D) Age
practice_questions.marks: B) Nationality of birth country [1 mark]. Note: Race (which includes nationality and ethnic origin) is a protected characteristic, but 'nationality of birth country' as a standalone category is not a precise protected characteristic listed in the Act. Examiners would credit responses demonstrating knowledge that race is protected while distinguishing the specific phrasing.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the term 'citizenship action'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that citizenship action involves citizens taking planned steps to bring about a change in policy, law or public life; 1 mark for developing this by noting that it can be carried out by individuals or groups and may target local, national or international issues.

practice_questions.text: Describe two methods used by citizens working through groups to challenge injustice, using examples from the case studies you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks (2 per method). Method 1: legal challenges through courts and inquests — for example, the Hillsborough families pursued new inquest proceedings that in 2016 returned unlawful killing verdicts, using the legal system alongside political campaigning (2 marks; 1 if identified but not developed or linked to a named example). Method 2: direct advocacy to MPs, ministers and parliamentary committees — for example, disability rights organisations including Scope submitted evidence to select committees, influencing the development of the Equality Act 2010 (2 marks; 1 if identified but not developed).

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below.

A fictional newspaper analysis piece from 2025 stated: 'Research tracking 40 citizen campaigns over a 20-year period found that campaigns combining legal action with sustained public advocacy were three times more likely to achieve their stated aims than those relying on a single method alone. The study also found that campaigns with a specific, focused aim outperformed those with broad or vague goals.'

Using the extract and your own knowledge, assess what this source tells us about what makes a citizenship action effective.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: 1 mark for identifying a relevant point from the source (e.g. using multiple methods increases the likelihood of success); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (e.g. campaigns that combine legal, political and public routes are more powerful than single-method ones); 1 mark for supporting this with own knowledge (e.g. the Hillsborough campaign combined legal processes and public lobbying; disability rights groups combined insider advocacy and public campaigns); 1 mark for a substantiated judgement that goes beyond the source (e.g. focus and persistence are also important factors, as demonstrated by campaigns that maintained a clear objective over many years).

practice_questions.text:
A community group is planning a campaign to improve facilities for young people in a local park that has been neglected. The group is debating whether to focus on direct action and public pressure or to work through formal channels such as council meetings and petitions.

Discuss the view that working through formal channels is the most effective way for citizens to bring about change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Well-developed two-sided discussion with specific named examples on each side (e.g. Hillsborough families using formal legal processes; disability rights groups using formal committee evidence, but also both using public campaigns). Uses connectives to weigh evidence and reaches a substantiated judgement about when formal channels are most or least effective.

Secure: Both sides covered with at least one developed point per side and one named example. Two-sided in places; generally accurate.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but develops unevenly; largely one-sided or without named examples.

Emerging: Basic points, little or no named example, descriptive.

practice_questions.text:
Evaluate the view that collective citizenship action — citizens working through groups — is a more effective way to bring about change than individual citizens acting alone.

In your answer, consider arguments in support of this view, arguments against it, and reach a substantiated overall judgement.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support: collective action provides greater resources, expertise and public profile than individuals can achieve alone; groups can sustain campaigns over time better than individuals; named examples show the power of collective action (Hillsborough Family Support Group over 30 years; disability rights organisations across multiple parliaments); groups can combine insider and outsider tactics simultaneously; collective campaigns attract media attention more effectively; they give marginalised communities a larger voice.

Arguments against: individual citizens can sometimes act faster and more flexibly than organisations; individual whistleblowers and campaigners (e.g. individuals who gathered and published evidence on corporate or state wrongdoing) can trigger change; groups can be divided or captured by internal politics; organised groups can represent narrow interests and may not speak for the communities they claim to represent.

Mastering: Sustained two-sided evaluation with named examples on both sides; weighs evidence; substantiated conclusion (e.g. collective action is generally more effective for sustained change against powerful institutions, but individuals can play a crucial catalytic role, particularly in triggering initial public awareness).

Secure: Both sides with at least one named example per side; reaches a conclusion but may not be fully substantiated.

Developing: Relevant points on both sides but limited development, or one-sided, or conclusion is a summary.

Emerging: Basic points, little real-world example, descriptive.

knowledge_checks.q: In which year were the original Hillsborough inquest verdicts quashed and new unlawful killing verdicts returned?
How many protected characteristics does the Equality Act 2010 cover?
The Hillsborough Independent Panel published a report in _____ confirming that 96 victims were unlawfully killed.
The Equality Act 2010 brought together previous laws on sex, race and disability discrimination into a single piece of _____.
Match each citizenship action element to its description:
right: The effect of a campaign on those it aimed to help
Speaking out publicly in support of a cause to change policy
A planned course of action by citizens to deliver a change for a community

flashcard_questions.q: When did the Hillsborough disaster occur?
flashcard_questions.a: 15 April 1989, at Hillsborough stadium in Sheffield.

flashcard_questions.q: What did the 2012 Hillsborough Independent Panel report conclude?
flashcard_questions.a: That 96 victims were unlawfully killed and there had been a cover-up.

flashcard_questions.q: What happened at the new Hillsborough inquest in 2016?
flashcard_questions.a: Juries returned unlawful killing verdicts for 96 of the 97 victims.
UK legislation that consolidated discrimination protections across nine protected characteristics.

flashcard_questions.q: How many protected characteristics does the Equality Act 2010 cover?
Name three protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010.
flashcard_questions.a: Any three from: age, disability, gender reassignment, race, religion or belief, sex, sexual orientation, pregnancy and maternity, marriage and civil partnership.
Planned, coordinated effort by citizens to achieve a specific change in policy, law or public life.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one feature shared by the Hillsborough and disability rights campaigns.
flashcard_questions.a: Both combined multiple methods (legal, political, media) and required sustained effort over many years.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the impact of a citizenship action?
flashcard_questions.a: The effect of the action on the individuals, groups or communities it aimed to help.

flashcard_questions.q: Which disability rights law preceded the Equality Act 2010?
What does 'advocacy' mean in a citizenship context?
flashcard_questions.a: Speaking out publicly in support of a cause to change attitudes or policy.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one method used by the Hillsborough Family Support Group.
flashcard_questions.a: Any one of: petitioning Parliament, legal proceedings, lobbying MPs, media engagement, gathering evidence.

glossary_terms.definition: Planned, coordinated effort by a group of citizens to achieve a specific change in policy, law or public life.
Personal characteristics protected from discrimination by law under the Equality Act 2010, including age, disability, gender reassignment, race, religion or belief, sex and sexual orientation.
Working with politicians, civil servants or organisations to influence a decision or policy, typically through meetings, evidence submissions or formal consultations.
The effect or consequence of a citizenship action on the individuals, groups, communities or systems it was intended to affect.
Coordinated effort by a group of people working together towards a shared goal, using their combined strength to achieve change that individuals could not accomplish alone.
Attempting to influence the decisions of politicians, civil servants or other decision-makers by presenting arguments, evidence or petitions directly to them.

items.title: BBC Witness History: Hillsborough
items.description: BBC World Service episode in which survivors and family members describe the events of 15 April 1989 and the long campaign for truth and accountability that followed.

items.title: Political Thinking with Nick Robinson: Justice Campaigns
items.description: Nick Robinson speaks with people involved in long-running justice campaigns, exploring how citizens sustain civic action over years and decades against powerful institutions.

items.title: We Need to Talk About an Injustice — Bryan Stevenson (TED)
items.description: Civil rights lawyer Bryan Stevenson on how sustained civic action and legal advocacy can challenge institutional injustice. A powerful parallel to the Hillsborough families' campaign.

items.title: Justice: What's a Fair Start? Episode 8 — Harvard University
items.description: Michael Sandel examines equal opportunity and structural disadvantage — the philosophical foundations behind disability rights legislation and campaigns like those that shaped the Equality Act 2010.

items.title: The Danger of a Single Story — Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie (TED)
items.description: Adichie's warning about how dominant narratives can silence marginalised voices — directly relevant to how the Hillsborough families had to fight a false official account for decades.

items.title: Hillsborough (1996 / 2016)
items.description: The original ITV drama by Jimmy McGovern, plus the 2016 BBC documentary revisiting the disaster and the decades-long campaign for justice. Essential viewing for this case study.

items.title: Just Mercy (2019)
items.description: The true story of Bryan Stevenson's legal campaigns to exonerate wrongly convicted prisoners in the USA. A powerful international parallel to the Hillsborough families' use of legal action and persistent civic advocacy.

items.title: Equality and Human Rights Commission: The Equality Act 2010
items.description: The EHRC's plain-English guide to all nine protected characteristics under the Equality Act 2010 — the legislation that resulted from years of disability rights and equality campaigns.

items.title: UK Parliament: Hillsborough — Parliamentary Debates and Reports
items.description: Hansard records and select committee reports on Hillsborough, showing how parliamentary scrutiny and civic lobbying contributed to the eventual justice outcomes.

items.title: Scope: Our History of Disability Rights Campaigning
items.description: Scope's account of the disability rights movement in the UK and how sustained campaigning contributed to the Disability Discrimination Act 1995 and the Equality Act 2010.

hero_image_caption: Citizens gathered together in collective support of a community justice campaign
